fields.label: City applying for
fields.ask: Ask which city they are applying to work in.

fields.label: Nursing qualification
fields.ask: Ask for their nursing qualification (for example GNM, ANM, B.Sc Nursing, Post Basic, Diploma) and the year they passed.

fields.label: Year of passing
fields.ask: Ask which year they passed that qualification.

fields.label: Height
fields.ask: Ask for their height and weight. Accept feet and inches or centimetres, and kilograms. Explain it is for the profile form only.

fields.label: Weight
fields.ask: Ask for their weight in kilograms.

fields.label: Years of nursing experience
fields.ask: Ask about their nursing experience: how many years in total, and where they worked. If they are a fresher, ask about hospital postings, internship or any patient-care exposure instead.

fields.label: Where they worked or what exposure they have
fields.ask: Ask where they worked (hospital ward, ICU, OT, home care, clinic) and what they did day to day. For freshers, ask what clinical exposure they had.

screening.care_intro: Explain that the role includes hands-on bedside care, such as bathing and hygiene, bedpan and toileting help, changing diapers for bedridden or elderly patients, and turning or lifting patients. Ask how comfortable they are doing this care.

care_items.label: changing diapers and incontinence care
care_items.ask: Ask directly whether they are comfortable changing diapers and doing incontinence care for adult patients.
persuasion: If they said they have never done it or can do other care instead, acknowledge that briefly — never done is okay. Then say diaper and incontinence care is still a required part of this role (dignity, skin health, preventing infection), done with gloves and training, and ask if they are willing to learn and do it.

Be kind and direct. Answer the one concern (never done / discomfort / prefer other duties): training will be given, but this duty cannot be skipped for other tasks. Ask for a clear yes or no: can they do diaper care as part of the job?

care_items.label: bed bath and personal hygiene care
care_items.ask: Ask if they are comfortable giving bed baths and personal hygiene care.

care_items.label: bedpan and toileting assistance
care_items.ask: Ask if they are comfortable helping patients with bedpan and toileting.

care_items.label: turning, lifting and repositioning patients
care_items.ask: Ask if they are comfortable turning, lifting and repositioning patients.

levels.seed: Ask the normal adult ranges for blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature, and which one would worry them most if it was off.

key_points.text: BP roughly 120/80 (acceptable about 90-140 / 60-90)
Pulse 60-100 per minute
Respiratory rate 12-20 per minute
Temperature about 36.5-37.5 C (97.7-99.5 F)
SpO2 95% or higher on room air

red_flags: States clearly unsafe ranges (for example normal pulse 40 or 160)
Says routine vitals do not need to be checked

levels.seed: Scenario: a patient's BP reads 80/50 and they feel dizzy. Ask what they do, step by step.

key_points.text: Keeps patient lying down, legs raised, safe from falling
Rechecks BP properly (manual or other arm) and checks pulse, SpO2, consciousness
Informs the doctor or senior nurse promptly
Looks for causes (bleeding, dehydration, medicines, sepsis)
Monitors frequently and documents

red_flags: Gives medicines on their own without an order
Does nothing or only waits and watches

levels.seed: Ask how they recognise that a ward patient is getting worse before it becomes an emergency, and what they do about it.

key_points.text: Looks at trends, not one reading; uses an early warning score if available
Knows rising respiratory rate and new confusion are early signs
Notes reduced urine output, skin colour, restlessness
Escalates early with a structured message (SBAR) or rapid response
Increases monitoring frequency

red_flags: Waits for the patient to collapse before calling anyone

levels.seed: Ask what checks they do before giving any medicine to a patient.

key_points.text: Right patient, confirmed with two identifiers
Right drug, dose, route and time checked against the order
Checks allergies
Checks label and expiry date
Documents after giving; explains to the patient

red_flags: Gives medicine without a doctor's order
Does not verify the patient's identity

levels.seed: Scenario: the prescribed dose looks much higher than usual. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Does not give it until clarified
Rechecks the order and calculation
Confirms with the prescribing doctor or pharmacist
Documents and reports; never changes the dose on their own

red_flags: Gives it anyway because the doctor wrote it
Changes the dose on their own

levels.seed: Scenario: they realise they gave a wrong medicine to a patient. Ask what they do straight away and afterwards.

key_points.text: Checks the patient and vital signs immediately
Informs doctor and senior at once
Monitors closely and follows orders for antidote or treatment
Documents honestly and files an incident report
Informs the patient or family as per policy

red_flags: Hides the error or says they would not report it

levels.seed: Ask when they wash their hands during patient care, and how.

key_points.text: Before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body-fluid exposure, after touching a patient, after touching surroundings
Soap and water about 40-60 seconds, or alcohol rub about 20-30 seconds when hands are not visibly dirty
Gloves do not replace hand washing

red_flags: Only washes at the end of the shift or only when hands look dirty

levels.seed: Ask how they dispose of used needles, soiled dressings and used gloves.

key_points.text: Needles and sharps go into a puncture-proof container (white or translucent), never recapped
Soiled dressings and body-fluid-contaminated items go to the yellow bag
Contaminated plastics such as tubing, catheters, gloves go to the red bag
Segregates at the point of generation; does not overfill containers

red_flags: Throws needles in normal dustbin
Recaps used needles by hand as routine

levels.seed: Scenario: they get a needle-stick injury from a used needle. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Washes the area immediately with soap and running water; does not squeeze hard or suck the wound
Reports to supervisor or infection control immediately
Gets medical evaluation and post-exposure prophylaxis as early as possible (ideally within hours)
Baseline and follow-up tests; checks hepatitis B vaccination status
Documents the incident

red_flags: Ignores it or delays reporting

levels.seed: Scenario: they find a patient on the floor who is not responding. Ask their first steps.

key_points.text: Checks the scene is safe
Checks responsiveness (tap and shout)
Calls for help or the emergency team and brings the crash cart or AED
Checks breathing and pulse for no more than about 10 seconds
Starts CPR if there is no breathing or pulse

red_flags: Leaves the patient to look for help without calling
Waits for a doctor before starting CPR

levels.seed: Ask them to explain how they do CPR on an adult: rate, depth and compression-to-breath ratio.

key_points.text: Hard, flat surface; hands on centre of the chest
Rate 100-120 per minute
Depth about 5-6 cm with full chest recoil
30 compressions to 2 breaths
Minimises interruptions, rotates compressors about every 2 minutes, uses AED as soon as available

red_flags: Would not start CPR without a doctor's order

levels.seed: Scenario: a patient's SpO2 drops to 85% and they are breathless. Ask what they do and in what order.

key_points.text: Sits the patient upright (Fowler's position)
Gives or increases oxygen as per protocol
Quickly checks airway, breathing, vitals and the likely cause
Calls the doctor or rapid response team
Prepares suction or ordered medicines, monitors continuously and documents

red_flags: Lays the breathless patient flat and leaves

areas.title: Bedridden patient care, hygiene and pressure injury

levels.seed: Ask how they prevent bedsores in a bedridden patient.

key_points.text: Repositions at least every 2 hours
Keeps skin clean and dry, checks pressure points (back of the hip, heels, elbows)
Keeps the bedsheet smooth; uses a pressure-relief mattress or pads
Ensures nutrition and hydration
Lifts rather than drags the patient (draw sheet)

red_flags: Says bedsores cannot be prevented
Massages red pressure areas hard

levels.seed: Ask them to walk through how they change a diaper for a bedridden adult, with hygiene and dignity.

key_points.text: Explains to the patient, ensures privacy (curtain or door)
Washes hands and wears gloves
Rolls the patient to the side, removes the soiled diaper, cleans front to back
Dries well, checks the skin for redness or rash, applies barrier cream if needed
Places the clean diaper, repositions, disposes of waste properly, washes hands, documents

red_flags: No gloves or hand hygiene
Rough or undignified handling

levels.seed: Scenario: a bedridden elderly patient has a red patch on the heel that stays red when pressed. Ask what it means and what they do.

key_points.text: Recognises an early (stage 1) pressure injury: non-blanchable redness
Relieves pressure (float the heels, reposition more often)
Reports and documents it
Keeps skin clean, supports nutrition, avoids massaging the area

red_flags: Rubs or massages the red area
Ignores it as normal

areas.title: IV line and urinary catheter care

levels.seed: Ask what they check at an IV cannula site.

key_points.text: Redness, swelling, pain, warmth (phlebitis)
Leakage or swelling around the site (infiltration)
Dressing intact and dry, insertion date noted
Line flows freely; changed per policy or when problems appear

red_flags: Says the site never needs checking

levels.seed: Scenario: a patient complains of burning pain at the IV site and the area is swollen. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Stops the infusion immediately
Does not flush or push more fluid into it
Removes the cannula per protocol and informs the doctor or senior
Re-sites in the other arm; elevates limb, assesses the extent; documents

red_flags: Continues the infusion

levels.seed: Ask how they care for a patient with a urinary catheter to prevent infection.

key_points.text: Keeps the closed drainage system; never disconnects without need
Bag always below bladder level and never on the floor
Hand hygiene; daily perineal hygiene
Secures the tube; empties the bag when about two-thirds full
Watches for cloudy or foul urine, fever and reports; catheter removed as soon as not needed

red_flags: Lifts the bag above the bladder
Opens the system routinely

levels.seed: Ask how they feed a weak patient who is lying in bed.

key_points.text: Sits the patient upright as much as possible
Small bites, slowly; waits for swallowing
Stops if coughing or choking; checks food temperature and consistency
Keeps the patient upright for a while after feeding

red_flags: Feeds a lying-flat patient quickly

levels.seed: Scenario: a patient starts coughing and turns blue while eating. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Stops feeding and calls for help
Encourages coughing if they can cough or speak
If they cannot breathe or speak: back blows and abdominal thrusts
Starts CPR if they become unresponsive; informs the doctor

red_flags: Gives water to wash it down

levels.seed: Ask how they give feeds through a nasogastric tube safely.

key_points.text: Confirms tube position before feeding (per protocol)
Head of bed raised 30-45 degrees during and after
Slow feed, flushes with water before and after
Stops if there is vomiting, distension or breathlessness and reports

red_flags: Feeds without checking tube position
Feeds with the patient lying flat

levels.seed: Scenario: a patient's relatives keep asking about the diagnosis, which the doctor has not explained yet. Ask what they say.

key_points.text: Respects confidentiality; does not share unauthorised details
Politely redirects to the doctor and offers to call the doctor
Shows empathy and does not give false hope

red_flags: Shares the full diagnosis themselves

levels.seed: Scenario: a confused elderly patient refuses medicine and gets angry. Ask how they handle it.

key_points.text: Stays calm; does not argue or force
Explains simply, reorients, tries again later or with a family member
Considers causes such as pain, infection, unfamiliar surroundings
Informs the doctor or senior and documents the refusal

red_flags: Forces the medicine
Mixes it secretly in food

levels.seed: Scenario: they see a colleague being rude to a patient or skipping hand washing. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Puts patient safety and dignity first
Speaks up respectfully, privately
Reports to the supervisor if it continues

red_flags: Ignores it as not their business

levels.seed: Ask why nurses document care, and what makes a good nursing note.

key_points.text: Legal record and continuity of care
Factual, objective, no guesses
Dated, timed and signed; written at the time of care
Corrections by a single line strike, never overwriting or erasing

red_flags: Writes notes for care that was not given

levels.seed: Ask how they hand over a patient to the next shift.

key_points.text: Structured handover (situation, background, assessment, recommendation)
Pending medicines, tests and tasks
Lines, drains, allergies, risks (fall, pressure injury)
Hands over at the bedside and allows questions

levels.seed: Scenario: they notice the previous shift did not record a medicine that may or may not have been given. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Does not give it again until verified
Checks with the colleague and the chart
Informs the in-charge and the doctor
Documents correctly as a late entry

red_flags: Gives the medicine again to be safe without checking

levels.seed: Ask what they check regularly for a patient on a ventilator.

key_points.text: Tube position, cuff and securement
SpO2, vitals, ventilator settings and alarms
Secretions and need for suction; sedation level
Head of bed raised 30-45 degrees and oral care to prevent ventilator pneumonia

red_flags: Silences alarms without checking the patient

levels.seed: Ask how they safely suction an intubated patient.

key_points.text: Hand hygiene, sterile gloves and catheter
Pre-oxygenates the patient
Suctions for no more than about 10-15 seconds, only while withdrawing
Watches SpO2 and heart rate; documents the secretions

red_flags: Suctions for long periods or uses non-sterile technique

levels.seed: Scenario: the ventilator high-pressure alarm goes off. Ask what they do.

key_points.text: Looks at the patient first, not the machine
Checks for secretions, biting or coughing, kinked or watery circuit, possible pneumothorax
Suctions if needed
If unresolved, disconnects and bags manually and calls the doctor or respiratory therapist

red_flags: Mutes the alarm and walks away

tiers.name: Tier 1 - Ready to deploy
tiers.description: Meets all screening requirements and shows solid, safe clinical knowledge at independent-practice level.
criteria: Screening complete and eligible (accepts essential care duties)
At least 2 years of relevant experience, or clearly strong clinical performance
Most assessed areas strong or adequate at intermediate level or above
No unsafe answers and no unresolved contradictions

tiers.name: Tier 2 - Deployable with support
tiers.description: Eligible with sound fundamentals but gaps in some areas; suitable with orientation or supervision.
criteria: Fundamentals correct; some partial answers at intermediate level

tiers.name: Tier 3 - Needs training
tiers.description: Eligible and willing, but limited experience or knowledge gaps in several basic areas.
criteria: Fresher or limited experience, or weak answers in several basic areas
Shows willingness and no unsafe practice

tiers.name: Not eligible
tiers.description: Does not meet a requirement of the role.
criteria: Declined an essential care duty after a respectful explanation, or
Gave answers that would put patients at risk, or
Material misrepresentation of experience or qualification

tiers.name: Needs human review
tiers.description: The AI cannot classify confidently, for example the audio was too poor, the interview ended early, or answers were too limited to assess.
criteria: Interview incomplete or heavily affected by audio problems
Too little evidence to classify without a human
